\chapter{A House, a Room, and the Stem That Bends}
\label{ch:mr-the-oblique-stem}
\hlchaptermodality{41}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a house and a room, and I can put either of them into the -t locative, knowing which one changes shape first and why.}

Complete MR-R41-in-the-house and answer kuṭhe? twice with a place you can name -- gharāt and khoolīt -- saying which of the two nouns had to bend.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ghar]{\mr{घर} (ghar) — house, home}

\label{lesson:MR-C41-ghar}



\begin{quote}
You can point at a place — \textbf{\mr{इथे}}, \textbf{\mr{तिथे}} — and you cannot yet NAME one.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ithe}, then \emph{tithe}, then ask \emph{kuṭhe?}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{घर}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{घर}} — \emph{ghar} — \textbf{house, home}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{माझं} \mr{घर} \mr{इथे} \mr{आहे}.} — \emph{mājhaṁ ghar ithe āhe.} — \textbf{my house is here.}
\end{quote}

Two letters you have had since chapter six, and a word Marathi uses for both \emph{house} and \emph{home} — the building and the belonging, with no second word for the difference.

It comes from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{गृह}} (\emph{gṛha}), and \textbf{\mr{गृह}} is built on the root \textbf{\mr{ग्रह्}} (\emph{grah-}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to grasp, to hold}.\textquotedblright{} You already own that root: it is the one under \textbf{\mr{घेणे}}, \emph{to take}. A house, in Marathi's oldest layer, is the thing that holds you.

\textbf{\mr{घर}} is \textbf{neuter}, like \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}}. That will matter the moment you put an adjective on it, and it matters now for \textbf{\mr{माझं}} rather than \emph{\mr{माझा}}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ghar} — house, home
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhaṁ ghar ithe āhe}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\mr{की}} and report that your house is here — \emph{mī mhaṇto kī …}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which taught verb shares a root with \textbf{\mr{घर}}? (\textbf{\mr{घेणे}} — both from \emph{grah-}, \textquotedblleft{}to hold\textquotedblright{}.) What gender is \textbf{\mr{घर}}? (\textbf{Neuter}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%98\%E0\%A4\%B0}{Wiktionary: \mr{घर}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[khoolī]{\mr{खोली} (khoolī) — room}

\label{lesson:MR-C41-kholi}



\begin{quote}
A house has an inside. That inside needs a name before anything can be said to be in it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{खोली}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{खोली}} — \emph{khoolī} — \textbf{room}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{माझ्या} \mr{घरात} \mr{एक} \mr{खोली} \mr{आहे}.} — \emph{mājhyā gharāt ek khoolī āhe.} — \textbf{there is one room in my house.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{खोली}} is \textbf{feminine}, which its \textbf{-\mr{ी}} ending announces before you are told. It is the word a rental notice uses, the word a hotel uses, and the word you would use for the room you sleep in — Marathi does not have a separate everyday noun for \emph{bedroom} the way English does; it says the room you do the sleeping in.

The word is the noun of \textbf{\mr{खोल}} (\emph{khool}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{deep}.\textquotedblright{} A room is a depth cut into a house. Once you know that pair you also know a second, unrelated-looking word: \textbf{\mr{खोली}} on its own can mean \emph{depth}, which is the same noun doing its literal job.

That sentence above did something new to \textbf{\mr{घर}}, and you should notice it now rather than be surprised by it: \textbf{\mr{घर}} became \textbf{\mr{घरा}-} before \textbf{-\mr{त}}. The next lesson is about nothing else.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{khoolī} — room
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhaṁ ghar; ek khoolī}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{-\mr{ण्यासाठी}} and give a purpose for a room — \emph{jhopaṇyāsāṭhī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What gender is \textbf{\mr{खोली}}, and what tells you? (\textbf{Feminine}; the \textbf{-\mr{ी}}.) What adjective is it built on? (\textbf{\mr{खोल}}, deep.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%96\%E0\%A5\%8B\%E0\%A4\%B2\%E0\%A5\%80}{Wiktionary: \mr{खोली}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gharā-]{\mr{घरा}- (gharā-) — the stem a noun takes before a postposition}

\label{lesson:MR-C41-oblique}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{घर}} became \textbf{\mr{घरात}} last lesson, and \textbf{\mr{पुणे}} became \textbf{\mr{पुण्यात}} back in chapter twelve. Neither one just took an ending. Both changed shape first.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the noun bends before anything is glued to it}]
Marathi puts almost every place, time and direction relation on a \textbf{post}position — a piece glued to the END of the noun. Chapter twelve showed you one. What it did not say is that the noun does not stay as it is: it first takes an \textbf{oblique stem}, and only then accepts the glue.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{घर}} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{घरा}-} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{घरात}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{पुणे}} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{पुण्या}-} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{पुण्यात}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{खोली}} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{खोली}-} $\to$ \textbf{\mr{खोलीत}}
\end{quote}

Three classes, three answers, and the pattern is worth holding as a shape rather than a list. A neuter noun ending in a consonant takes \textbf{-\mr{आ}}. A noun ending in \textbf{-\mr{ए}} takes \textbf{-\mr{या}}. A feminine noun in \textbf{-\mr{ी}} does not change at all.

This is the single most load-bearing rule in the book so far, because nothing in the next three chapters works without it. Every one of the five postpositions they teach — \emph{madhye}, \emph{var}, \emph{khālī}, \emph{javaḷ} and \emph{samor} — demands the oblique before it, and a Marathi sentence that skips it is not merely clumsy: it is wrong.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ghar}, then \emph{gharāt} — and hear the extra \emph{ā}
  \item \emph{khoolī}, then \emph{khoolīt} — and hear that nothing was added
  \item \emph{mī gharāt rāhto} — I live in the house
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happens to a Marathi noun before a postposition? (\textbf{It takes an oblique stem first}.) Which of the three classes changes least? (\textbf{Feminine -\mr{ी}} — not at all.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gharāt · khoolīt]{Ask where, and answer with a place you can name}

\label{lesson:MR-R41-in-the-house}



\begin{quote}
Until this chapter, \textbf{\mr{कुठे}?} could only be answered by pointing. Now it can be answered with a room.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kuṭhe āhe?} — then answer \emph{gharāt}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the same question answered \emph{khoolīt}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ithe} — and notice you can now answer that question two ways
  \item \emph{Recall:} say a \emph{jevhā … tevhā …} sentence about being at home
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the line of your message that means \emph{I understand Marathi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \textbf{\mr{घर}} and \textbf{\mr{खोली}} changes shape before \textbf{-\mr{त}}? (\textbf{\mr{घर}}, to \textbf{\mr{घरा}-}.) Why does that rule matter more than it looks? (\textbf{Every postposition in the next three chapters needs it}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
